Write a short letter to the person today. Tell them what has happened since they left, what you wish you had said, what you are thankful for. You do not have to send it or show anyone. Some words only need to leave your chest and land on paper.

Losing someone changes your daily routine in places you did not expect: the missed call at the usual time, the empty chair, the extra plate. Notice these moments without judging them. They show how much that person was woven into your days. It is natural for them to hurt.

Think of three things you learned from them. Maybe how to greet people, how to save, how to laugh at trouble. Write them down. Grief hurts because the love was real, and these lessons are one way that love keeps living in you.

There is no rule that says you must be at the family gathering, at church or mosque, or at work with a calm face. If you cannot cope with an event today, send a short message and rest. Looking after yourself is not disrespect to the person you lost.

Friends may not know what to say, so they say nothing or say the wrong thing. You can help by being direct: 'I do not need advice. I just need you to sit with me for a while.' Most people are relieved to be told what actually helps.

A small ritual can give grief somewhere to go. Light a candle in the evening, say a short prayer, or mention one memory aloud. Do it at the same time each day if it helps. Rituals do not erase the pain, but they give it a gentle place to rest.

Should grief feel too heavy to carry alone for weeks, and daily life is slipping away, please speak to a counsellor, a pastor or imam you trust, or a Therapia therapist. Asking for help is not a sign that you are failing. It is a way of looking after yourself while you carry something big.

Not every loss gets public mourning: a miscarriage, a friend, a pet, a relationship that ended in silence. Your grief is still real even if there was no ceremony. Give yourself your own small ceremony today, in whatever way feels right.

On hard days, shrink the day. Do not think about next month or next year. Ask: what is the next hour? Bathe, eat, answer one call, sit outside for five minutes. When that hour is done, ask again. Getting through a day this way is real progress.

Guilt often travels with grief: I should have called, I should have taken them to hospital sooner. Hindsight gives clarity you did not have then. You made choices with the information, money and strength you had. Speak to yourself the way you would speak to a friend in your place.

Look at where you were a month ago. Maybe you can now eat a full meal, or speak about them without breaking down, or attend a gathering. Maybe not yet, and that is fine too. Progress in grief is not a straight line, but small shifts are worth noticing.

Is there something of theirs you would like to keep close, a cloth, a photo, a recipe, a voice note? Keep it safe today. And if looking at their things is too painful right now, there is no rush to sort them. Nothing has to be decided or cleared until you are ready.

Faith and grief can sit together uneasily. You may pray and still feel empty, or feel angry at God and then guilty for it. Many people go through that. Honest feelings are not betrayal. You can bring them just as they are, and take your time.

In the first weeks after a loss, life can feel like it is happening behind glass. Do the basics: water, food, a bath, a little sunlight. Let others handle what they can. You are not required to understand everything yet, only to get through today, and that is enough.
addiction: Just for today. That is the only day you have to win.
A craving is a wave. It rises, peaks, and passes.
A slip is a stumble, not the end of your effort.
Drink water and eat breakfast. Hunger can make cravings louder.
Tell one safe person how today is going.
You are more than your worst night.
Delay it by ten minutes. Then decide again.
Stay away from the places that pull you back, just for today.
Needing help is not weakness. It is good sense.
Every sober hour counts, not only the long streaks.
Walk around the compound or street for ten minutes before deciding anything.
Notice one thing that is better this week than last month.
Choose one person to call when the evening gets hard.
Rest well tonight. Tiredness makes urges stronger.
Be honest with yourself this morning. Honesty is where change starts.
Cravings often come at the same time each day, like after work or on weekends. Think about your hardest hour and plan one thing to do in it, like a call, a walk, or a meal.
When friends offer a drink or a smoke, you can say, 'No, I am good,' and change the subject. You do not owe anyone an explanation.
Stopping heavy alcohol or drug use suddenly can be dangerous for some people. Please talk to a doctor or counsellor before you cut down on your own.
Shame says hide. Support says speak. Tell someone you trust one true thing about how you are doing today.
If you slipped yesterday, do not wait for Monday or a new month to begin again. You can start again this morning.
Money spent on drink or drugs adds up. Today, think of one thing you would rather use that money for. Write it down and keep it where you can see it.
Weekends, festivals and owambe parties can be tricky. Decide beforehand how long you will stay, what you will drink instead, and who you can step outside and call.
Look back at the last time a craving passed without you giving in. What did you do? That is proof you can ride it out again.
Boredom and loneliness often sit behind a craving. Ask yourself what you are really needing right now: rest, food, company, or comfort.
A worried family member may sound angry. Often it is fear. Try listening to them for two minutes without defending yourself.
Keep a few things at hand for tough moments: a cold drink, a song, a number to call, a short prayer. Prepare them while you are calm.
You may feel you have to do this alone. You do not. A support group, a counsellor, or one honest friend can make hard days lighter.
Some people use drink or drugs to cope with stress, grief or worry about money. When you find a gentler way to cope, the urge loses some of its power.
Do not measure yourself against anyone else's journey. Your only comparison is you yesterday.
Throw out or give away what you keep at home that tempts you. Making it harder to reach gives you time to think.
Treat yourself kindly when you do well. A good meal, a clean shirt, a short rest. Recovery is hard work, and small rewards help.
Not everyone will understand. Some may still joke about your past. You can choose which people get close to you right now.
Notice how your body feels in the morning without a hangover or a comedown. Even a small improvement is worth noticing.
Pick a new activity for the time you used to spend drinking or using: football with neighbours, an evening class, a church or mosque group, or a walk. Fill the space on purpose.
When people ask why you stopped, you can keep it short: 'It was not helping me.' That is enough.
Healing from addiction often happens in ordinary moments, like saying no at a gathering or going home early. Notice those moments today. They matter more than they seem.

Try urge surfing. When a craving hits, do not fight it. Sit down and watch it like a wave. Notice where you feel it in your body, and how strong it is from one to ten. Keep breathing slowly. Many cravings rise and fall in a short time. After it passes, notice that you stayed in charge.

If you slip, here is a plan. First, be safe: drink water, eat, and avoid further use if you can. Second, do not punish yourself with shame. Third, tell someone you trust or your counsellor. Fourth, ask what led up to it. A slip gives you information, and it does not erase the days you have already done.

Please do not stop heavy or long-term alcohol or drug use suddenly without advice from a doctor or trained professional, because withdrawal can be risky for some people. Going slowly with support is not cheating. It is protecting yourself. A clinic or a Therapia counsellor can help you work out a safe next step.

Write down three reasons you want to change. Not what others want, but yours: your health, your children, your business, your peace of mind. Fold the paper and keep it in your wallet or phone. On a hard day, read it before you do anything else.

Think about who is in your corner: a sibling, a friend, a pastor, a colleague. Choose one and tell them what you are working on. Ask for something small, like a daily check-in message. Being accountable to one person can be lighter than carrying the secret alone.

Evenings are often the hardest time. Make a simple evening plan today: when you will eat, who you will call, what you will watch or listen to, and when you will go to bed. A plan made in the morning is easier to follow than a decision made in the middle of a craving.

Some people think they must hit rock bottom before they can change. You do not. You can decide today that enough is enough, before you lose more of your health, money or relationships. Any day you choose to begin is a good day to begin.

Rebuilding trust with family takes time. Words help, but small, steady actions help more: showing up on time, keeping promises, being present at meals. You cannot rush their healing, but you can keep showing up. Let them see the change slowly.

Sleep, food and movement all affect cravings. If you are skipping meals or staying awake until 3 a.m., urges may feel stronger. Today try one simple thing: eat at regular times, or be in bed by a set hour. Look after the basics and the hard parts get a little easier.

Your craving is a thought, not an order. You can think, 'I want to drink' and still choose not to. Try saying to yourself, 'I notice I am having the urge.' That small distance gives you room to choose. You have made that choice before, and you can make it again.

Should you be using drugs or alcohol and think you might harm yourself, or you feel unsafe, please tell someone near you right now and go to the nearest clinic or hospital. You do not have to wait until things improve. Your life matters more than how you look to others.

Quick relief from alcohol or drugs often costs more later: money, sleep, trust, health. Today, think about what you want your next year to look like. Then ask whether what you are about to do takes you closer or further. You do not have to be perfect. You only need to face the right direction.

Count what has changed since you started trying: days sober, money kept, clearer mornings, fewer arguments, better sleep. Write the list. Progress in recovery can be quiet and easy to miss. On days you feel nothing is working, this list can show you what is.

Recovery is not a punishment, and it is not a test of your character. It is learning new ways to handle stress, sadness and joy. You are allowed to be a beginner at that. Be patient with yourself the way you would be with a child learning to walk.
habits: Charge your phone outside the bedroom tonight.
An urge is not a command. Let it pass like a wave.
You are not broken for struggling with this.
Delay it by ten minutes. Stand up and move to another room.
Put the phone face down for the first hour of the day.
Cold water on your face can break an urge.
Today, one small win is enough.
Slipping once does not erase your progress.
Open a book, or a voice note from a friend, before opening social media.
Shame feeds the habit. Kindness helps you change it.
Notice the moment before you reach for your phone.
Try going outside for five minutes with no phone.
Ask what you were feeling just before the urge came.
Log out of one app today. Small friction helps.
Be honest with yourself and gentle at the same time.
Many people use porn or endless scrolling to escape stress, loneliness or boredom. When the urge comes, ask what you really need: rest, company, a break, or comfort.
Phones in bed make late nights longer. Try a simple rule: charge it across the room, use a cheap alarm clock, and see how your mornings feel after one week.
Delete the apps or bookmarks that pull you in, or move them off your home screen. Making it harder to reach gives your better judgement time to show up.
Urge surfing: when the urge comes, stay still, breathe, and watch it rise and fall like a wave. You do not have to act on it. Many urges soften if you wait.
Choose a replacement for the moment you usually reach for it: push-ups, a short walk, a call to a friend, or tidying your room. Decide now so it is ready.
Turn off notifications that are not from real people. Each buzz is a small pull. Fewer pulls leave more attention for your day.
Being alone in a room late at night with data on is the high-risk time. Plan ahead: stay in common areas, keep the door open, or sleep earlier.
Check how many hours you spend on your phone each day. Do not judge yourself, just look at the number. Awareness is the first step to adjusting it.
Porn can change how we see ourselves and other people. If you want to step back from it, you are not being dramatic. It is okay to want a calmer, more honest relationship with desire.
Tell one trusted friend or counsellor about your goal. Secrets make urges stronger. Even a short honest message can lighten the load.
Set one phone-free time today, maybe meals or the first thirty minutes after waking. Start small so you can keep it going.
Switch your screen to black and white in the evening, or set a daily limit on the apps that eat your time. The goal is not punishment, just a gentle nudge.
When you slip, skip the long lecture to yourself. Say, 'That happened. What led up to it?' Then make one small change for next time.
Data bundles are expensive, and so is your time. Think about what a week of less scrolling could give you: sleep, savings, or finishing something you started.
Find what fills the empty hours: football, a course, a side hustle, a church or mosque youth group, learning a skill. A full life leaves less room for the habit.
Social media can make everyone's life look better than yours. Try following fewer accounts that leave you feeling small, and more that teach or inspire you.
Early signs matter: feeling tired, lonely, stressed, or bored. Catching the feeling early gives you more choice than catching it after the urge is strong.
Fewer relapses, shorter sessions, or longer gaps between them are all progress worth counting. You do not need to be perfect to improve.
Watch for the thought 'just this once' or 'a quick look'. A quick look can turn into an hour. Name the thought and then do your replacement action.
Your worth has nothing to do with this habit. You can be a good person and still be learning to change a pattern.

Make your phone a little less tempting tonight. Charge it outside your bedroom. Set a time after which you stop using it, say 10 p.m. Put a book, a Bible, a Quran, or a notepad near your bed. Tomorrow morning, notice how you slept and how you feel. If it helps, keep it going for a week.

Try the five-minute rule. When an urge comes, tell yourself you can have it in five minutes, but first you will stand, drink water and walk to a different room. When time is up, check how strong the urge is. Often it has faded. If not, wait five more minutes.

Think about what the habit gives you in the moment. Escape? Relief? Company? Then look for a healthier way to get the same thing. If it is relief, try slow breathing or a walk. If it is company, call a friend or visit family. When you meet the need directly, the habit has less to offer.

If porn has affected your relationship, work, or sleep, you are not alone, and it is not too late to change. Be honest about how much of it you want to cut and why. Then take one concrete step today: block sites, tell someone, or arrange to speak to a counsellor. You do not need to carry this by yourself.

Create a simple morning routine that does not start with your phone. Wake up, drink water, wash your face, pray or stretch, and eat. Only then check messages. The first thing your mind takes in sets the tone for the day, and a calmer start can make scrolling feel less urgent.

Many people try to quit with willpower alone and feel like failures when it does not work. Willpower gets tired. Change your surroundings instead: use website blockers, keep your phone out of the bathroom, remove saved links, avoid idle time. Make the habit harder and the better choice easier.

A relapse is a lesson, not a verdict. Ask: what time was it, where was I, how was I feeling, what did I do just before? Write the answers down. Next time you will recognise the pattern earlier. Then forgive yourself and get on with the day. Shame will only push you back to the screen.

Phones are built to keep you scrolling. Endless feeds, autoplay and red dots are designed to hold your attention, so struggling with them says nothing about your character. You can use your phone for what you choose, such as calls, learning, work, and family. Start by deciding two things you will use it for today.

Try a phone-free hour this evening. Eat dinner with family, visit a neighbour, cook, or play a game. At first the quiet may feel uncomfortable, and you may reach for your phone out of habit. That is normal. Stay with it for the hour and notice how it feels once the restlessness settles.

Loneliness drives many screen habits. If you live alone or far from family, it is easy to fill the evening with a screen. Today, reach out to one real person by voice note or call. Even a short chat can ease the pull to scroll or watch something you will regret.

Make a list of what you would do with an extra hour a day: study, exercise, build your side business, pray, rest, or be with loved ones. Put the list where you will see it. When you feel like scrolling, check the list and pick one. Over time, your hours start to match your goals.

Stuck in a cycle of promising and failing? Try changing the goal. Instead of 'never again', aim for 'today'. Instead of aiming to feel no urges, aim to respond to them differently. Smaller goals are easier to reach and give you something to build on.

Speak to someone if this habit is taking over your life or making you feel hopeless. A counsellor, a trusted elder, or a Therapia therapist will not shock easily. They have heard this before. Talking about it openly can take away much of its power and help you plan your next step.

Notice when you pick up your phone without any reason. Pause, take a breath, and ask, 'What am I looking for?' Sometimes the answer is a message from someone, but often it is a break from a feeling. Naming the feeling, such as tired or anxious, can make it easier to deal with directly.

Set small, specific rules instead of vague promises. For example: no phone at the table, no social media before work is done, no screens in bed. Tell someone about your rules. After a week, review what worked and adjust. Little rules, kept consistently, add up to a real change.
money: Write down every naira you spend today. Just notice.
Small savings still count. Keep what you can, even N200.
Your worth is not your account balance.
Before you buy, wait one day. Then decide.
Check your balance before you plan the day's spending.
Name one thing you can do today to improve your money situation.
Money stress is heavy. Talking about it can help.
Walk past the sale. Your plan matters more.
Pay yourself first, even if it is a small amount.
Quick money schemes that promise to double your money are usually a trap.
Cook at home today and see how much you keep.
Ask the price at two places, then compare.
Progress with money is slow, and slow is fine.
Look at one subscription or habit you can cut this week.
Be kind to yourself about past money choices.
Make a list of what you must pay this month: rent, food, transport, data, school fees. Put the must-haves first. A clear list can calm the fear of the unknown.
Prices keep rising, and that is stressful. You are not failing if your money does not stretch as far as before. Focus on the few things you can control today.
Try putting a small amount aside as soon as you receive money, before you spend. Even a little each week builds a cushion for emergencies.
Loan apps may seem to solve a problem fast, but the high interest and harassment can make things worse. If you are tempted, speak to someone you trust first.
Ajo or esusu groups can help with discipline and saving. Join only people you trust, agree on the rules clearly, and keep records.
Family may ask you for money you do not have. It is okay to say, 'I cannot do that now, but I will help when I can.' Saying no kindly is not selfishness.
Separate business money from personal money, even if you only use two envelopes or two accounts. It will show you the real picture.
Check the cost of data, transport, and airtime this week. Small leaks add up. Find one to reduce without making life miserable.
If you owe people, list who, how much, and when. Then contact the smaller debts first and offer a realistic plan. Many people prefer an honest plan to silence.
Compare prices at two places before buying food items. A few minutes can save you real money over the month.
Do not compare your finances with what people show on social media. You do not see their debts or their struggles.
An emergency fund does not need to be big at first. Start with enough for one day's food, then two days, then a week.
Be careful of people who ask you to send money first to get a big return. Real opportunities do not rush you or hide the details.
Learn one skill that people will pay for, like tailoring, phone repair, braiding, spreadsheets, or tutoring. Spend a little time on it today.
Talk to your partner or family about money plans calmly. Surprises about spending often cause the biggest arguments.
Feeling ashamed about money is common. It does not mean you have done something wrong. Many people are working things out behind the scenes.
Set a small weekly target, such as saving N500 or reducing one expense. Reaching small targets builds confidence.
Only lend friends what you can afford to lose, and be honest about it. That protects both the money and the friendship.
Keep your plans simple. A budget you can follow is better than a perfect one you abandon in three days.
Remember what you have already survived financially. You have found ways through before, and you can find a way again.

Try the 'three lists' exercise. List what you earn, what you must spend, and what you want to spend. Look at where the numbers do not match. Choose one change, such as reducing airtime, cooking more, or delaying a purchase. You do not need to fix everything. One small change this week is enough to start.

When money is tight, the mind goes to the worst case. Write down what you are afraid of, then next to it write one thing you can do about it. For example: 'I may not pay rent', then 'I will speak to my landlord on Friday.' Fear shrinks a little when it has a next step attached.

Many people lose money to schemes that promise to double it in weeks. Before you put any money in, ask: who is paying the returns, can I withdraw whenever I want, and is it registered? If it sounds too good to be true, step back. Slow, ordinary progress is safer than a dream that leaves you with nothing.

Debt can make you want to avoid your phone. But silence usually makes things worse. Write down what you owe and to whom. Then reach out to the one who is most patient and propose a small, regular payment you can keep. A small steady plan shows good faith and often opens a conversation.

Your value as a person does not depend on how much you earn. A good name, kindness, honesty, and effort all matter. When someone's opinion of you is tied to money, remember that it says something about their view, not your worth. Hold your head up today.

Try a no-spend hour, or a no-spend day. Before opening your wallet or transfer app, ask: do I need this or only want it? Is there a cheaper way? Will I still care in a week? You may still buy it, but you will buy it on purpose. That small pause protects more money than you think.

If you have a small business or side hustle, track three things each day: what you spent, what you sold, and what remains. Five minutes at night in a notebook is enough. After a month you will see which items bring profit and which only look busy. Decisions get easier when you know your numbers.

Talking about money with family can feel awkward, but it helps. Choose a calm time. Say what you can afford, what you cannot, and what you are working on. Ask for their help in making a plan rather than making a demand. Open conversations often reduce pressure.

Saving does not have to be perfect. If you miss a week, restart. If you must dip into savings for a real emergency, that is what it is for. Just try to refill it later. The habit matters more than the amount. Over months, small deposits become a safety net you can count on.

When fuel or food prices rise, it is natural to feel anxious. Try listing three ways you have already adapted. Then pick one more adjustment, like sharing transport, buying in bulk with a neighbour, or planning meals. You are more resourceful than you feel today.

Credit and loan apps can trap people with high interest and threats to contact your family. If you are already in one, do not borrow from a second app to pay the first. Write down the amounts, and speak to someone you trust or a counsellor about a plan. There are ways forward, and you do not have to face it alone.

Before sending money to relatives or friends, decide your limit for the month and keep to it. Tell them honestly if you have reached it. Giving from what you can afford keeps your generosity sustainable. Giving beyond your means can leave you needing help yourself.

Set one money goal for the next three months that is specific and small: build an emergency fund of N10,000, pay off one debt, or learn one skill. Write it down and break it into weekly steps. Check on it each Sunday. Progress you can see keeps you motivated.

If money worries keep you awake, write them down before bed, then close the notebook. Tell yourself you will look at it tomorrow with fresh eyes. Worry at night can make problems look bigger. In the morning, pick one item and take one step. A tired mind is not the best place to solve money problems.

Money is a tool, and a tight season does not define your future. Keep being honest, keep learning, and keep taking small steps. Look at how far you have come, even if the progress is not what you hoped for. You are allowed to be proud of surviving a hard time with your dignity intact.
jobloss: Having no job right now does not make you worthless.
Get up, wash, and dress as if the day matters. It does.
Send one message to someone about work today.
Rejection is about fit and timing, not your value.
Write down three skills you have. Employers pay for skills.
Take a short walk. A clear head helps.
One application, one call, one message. That is a good day.
Rest is not laziness when you are carrying this much.
Ask someone you trust if they know of any openings.
Beware of any job offer that asks you to pay first.
Keep a routine. It protects your mood.
Your CV can be improved today in just thirty minutes.
You are allowed to feel afraid and still keep trying.
Learn one new thing for free today.
Small steps count, even when the waiting is long.
Set a simple daily routine: wake up at a fixed time, spend a couple of hours on job search or skills, then rest or help at home. Structure keeps the days from blurring.
Tell your friends and family what kind of work you are looking for. Many jobs and contracts come through people, not job boards.
Update your CV and make it one clean page. List what you did, not just where you were. Ask a friend to read it for mistakes.
Job adverts that ask for registration fees, training fees, or your bank details early deserve caution. Real employers do not charge you to be considered.
If you can, take on small paid work while you search: deliveries, tutoring, selling, repairs, or writing. It brings in some money and keeps you active.
People may ask, 'Have you found something yet?' You can say, 'I am working on it, and I will tell you when there is news.' You do not owe more.
Losing a job can feel like losing your identity. Remind yourself of who you are beyond work: a friend, a parent, a believer, a person with talents.
Cut your expenses to the essentials for now, and tell the people close to you why. Honest talks reduce pressure and arguments.
Take time today to learn a skill online or at a local centre: Excel, digital marketing, tailoring, phone repair, or basic coding. Pick one and spend an hour.
Reach out to a former colleague or boss and ask for advice or a reference. Many people are glad to help when asked politely.
Interviews are practice too. After each, write one thing that went well and one thing to improve. Each one makes the next one easier.
Avoid taking loans from apps to cover living costs while you search. High interest can turn a hard season into a harder one.
Family or community may pressure you with expectations. You can say, 'I am doing all I can, and I would appreciate your support.' It is a fair request.
A long search can drain your energy. Plan something free and enjoyable each week, like a walk, football, or time with friends, so life is not only about the search.
Sleep and food matter even more now. Try to keep regular meal times and a regular bedtime. Your mind works better when your body is looked after.
Think about what you could offer people directly: cleaning, designing, translating, cooking, event help. You may find your first paying customer closer than you think.
Notice your self-talk today. If you hear 'I am useless,' replace it with 'I am between jobs and learning what is next.' Words shape the mood of your day.
If you were laid off, it was a business decision and not a verdict on your character. Many capable people lose jobs through no fault of their own.
Ask one person each day for a short chat about their work. You learn about opportunities, and you stay connected to the working world.
Join a local group, a church or mosque network, or an online community in your field. Opportunities and encouragement often come from belonging.

Make a simple weekly plan. Monday and Tuesday: apply to jobs. Wednesday: contact three people. Thursday: learn a skill. Friday: follow up on applications. Weekend: rest and spend time with family. A plan gives each day a purpose, and you can see progress even when no offer has come yet.

Practise answering the question 'Tell me about yourself' out loud. Keep it to about a minute: who you are, what you have done, what you can offer, and what you are looking for. Say it to a mirror or a friend. The more you practise, the more calmly you will speak when the real interview comes.

When months pass with no work, shame can creep in. You may avoid gatherings or skip calls. But you are not the only one. Many skilled people in Nigeria are searching right now. Try telling one person honestly how you are doing. Sharing the burden does not make you look weak. It reminds you that you are not alone.

Look at your last job and list ten things you did, including small ones: handled customers, fixed problems, trained a colleague, met deadlines. These are your skills in plain language. Use them in your CV and when you speak to people. You will see you have more to offer than you thought.

Not every opportunity looks like a full-time job. Consider contract work, apprenticeship, volunteering, or starting small with what you already know. These can bring income, experience, and contacts. They may also lead to something more permanent. Start with one option this week and see where it goes.

Fear of the future can take over when the days are quiet. Try this: write the fear down, then write what you can control today. You cannot control whether a company replies, but you can control whether you send the application, prepare for the call, or ask for advice. Put your energy there.

If you have a spouse or children depending on you, the pressure can feel heavy. Speak with them honestly about the situation and what you are doing. Ask for their patience and ideas. Often, family members can help in ways you did not expect, and open talks reduce hidden resentment.

Be wary of anyone who promises you a job abroad or a high-paying role in exchange for money upfront. Check the company yourself, ask for written details, and talk to someone who has dealt with them. Desperation makes people vulnerable to scams, so it is wise to slow down, even when the offer is tempting.

Long job searches can drain your mood. Please look after your mind. Go outside daily, move your body, eat properly, and talk to someone. If you feel hopeless for many days, or have thoughts of harming yourself, speak to a counsellor, a Therapia therapist, or someone you trust right away. You deserve support.

Your skills may fit more than one field. A customer service worker may do well in sales, an accountant in bookkeeping for small shops, a teacher in training or tutoring. Take a fresh look at what you can transfer. Widening your search a little can open doors you did not see before.

Following up politely can set you apart. A week after applying or interviewing, send a short message: thank them, restate your interest, and ask about the next step. Keep it respectful and brief. Even if the answer is no, you will have left a good impression, and some people remember it later.

Take stock of the money you have and how long it can last. Write a bare-bones budget: food, rent, transport, data. Seeing the real numbers can be scary, but it also gives you a plan. Then you can decide what to reduce and when you need income, which helps you make calm decisions rather than panicked ones.

Think back to a hard time you got through. What did you do? Who helped? What did you learn? Write a few lines. Those strengths did not go anywhere when your job did. They are still with you, and they will help you again. Let that memory give you a little courage for today's step.

Dignity does not come from a salary. It comes from how you treat people, how you keep your word, and how you keep going when things are hard. Today you may not have a title, but you can still show up with honesty and effort. That is who you are, whatever your payslip says.

When you get an interview, prepare simply. Learn what the company does, think of two questions to ask, choose your outfit the night before, and plan how you will get there on time, allowing for traffic. Preparation will not guarantee an offer, but it will help you feel steadier and speak more clearly.
work: You do not have to fix the whole job today. Just the next task.
A hard day at work does not mean you are bad at your job.
Drink some water before you open the first email. Small things count.
Leave on time today if you can. Rest is part of doing good work.
Your worth is bigger than your job title.
One difficult conversation put off is one more night of worry.
Tired of the commute? Choose one small thing to enjoy on the road.
Nobody knows everything at work. Asking a question is a skill.
Pick the one task that matters most and do it before ten o'clock.
Most mistakes at work can be fixed. Breathe first, then plan.
Notice one thing you did well this week, however small.
Not every message needs an answer this very minute.
Take a real lunch break. Your mind needs it as much as your body.
Your boss's mood is not a report on your value.
Job hunting is tiring. Rest between applications.

When a day feels too heavy, shrink it. Ask what the next hour needs from you, and only that. Plenty of difficult days become manageable one hour at a time. Then tomorrow, you can take it one hour at a time again.
If your boss is hard to deal with, keep a short note of what was agreed after each meeting. It protects your peace and makes later conversations clearer.

Feeling behind at work is very common, especially when you are carrying more than your share. It does not mean you are failing. It may mean the load is too big. Try telling your manager what is taking time. Quiet struggle helps nobody.
Before you reply to an annoying message, wait ten minutes. Walk, stretch, or drink water. Your answer will usually be calmer and more useful.

Comparing your career to a classmate or cousin who seems ahead is a quiet way to lose joy. Their story has parts you cannot see. Yours is still being written. Choose one small skill to build this month and measure only against your own yesterday.
A tip for asking for help: be specific. Instead of saying you are overwhelmed, say which two tasks you cannot finish this week and ask what can wait.

Power cuts, traffic, slow networks. Many things that disturb your work are outside your control. Name one thing you can control today and give it your attention. Even five minutes of calm focus is worth more than an hour of frustration.
It is allowed to want more from your job, whether that is better pay, respect, or growth. Wanting more does not make you ungrateful.
If you made a mistake yesterday, say so plainly, offer the fix, and move on. People usually remember how you handled it more than the mistake itself.

Sunday evening dread is a real feeling, and many people share it. Try planning one small pleasant thing for Monday, like a favourite meal or a call with a friend. It does not have to be big. A small plan is enough to soften the start of the week.
Being the one who always says yes can wear you down. Practise a kind no today: I cannot take that on right now, but I can look at it on Thursday.
Is there a colleague you can trust, even one? A few honest minutes with someone who understands your workplace can lighten the whole week.
Your job pays your bills, but it is not all of you. Spend a few minutes today on something that has nothing to do with work.

Feeling invisible at work is painful. Consider writing down your wins each week. It helps you remember them, and gives you words when it is time to speak up. Little notes, kept over months, can show you how far you have come.

Fear of losing your job can follow you everywhere. Try writing down the worry, then one small step you could take, such as updating your CV or speaking with someone in your field. Doing something, however small, often loosens the grip of the fear.

If you are overloaded, try the three-list method. Write what must be done today, what can wait until this week, and what can be dropped. Seeing it on paper often calms the mind. Then start with only the first list. The rest can wait its turn.

Working long hours can feel like proof of commitment, but tired minds make more errors and enjoy less. Today, choose a clear stopping time and stick to it as best you can. Your best work comes from a mind that has been allowed to rest.

Some bosses give feedback in a harsh way. Try separating the tone from the content. Ask yourself what useful point is inside, take it, and let the rest go. You can also ask them calmly to be specific. You can learn from criticism without letting it hurt your sense of who you are.
Think back to a work problem that once felt impossible. You got through it. That same ability is still with you today, even if you do not feel it right now.
Before a big meeting, take one slow breath in for four counts and out for six. Do it three times. Then remember that being prepared is enough. You do not need to be perfect.

Many people in Nigeria carry family expectations along with work stress, supporting relatives while trying to build their own life. That is heavy. You are allowed to feel tired, and allowed to ask for understanding. Be patient with the person who is holding so much.
When you are stuck on a task, change something small: stand up, move seats, or step outside for two minutes. A short break often unlocks what more effort cannot.

Try a short end-of-day ritual. Write down tomorrow's top three tasks, close your notebook or laptop, and tell yourself work is finished for now. It helps your mind stop chasing the job at home. Over time, this small habit can make your evenings feel like your own again.

Starting a new job can feel like being lost. Give yourself months, not days, to feel settled. Ask questions early, write down what you learn, and be patient with yourself while you grow. Nobody is born knowing a workplace. Everyone started somewhere.
Being laid off or between jobs is not a verdict on who you are. It is a hard season. Keep a simple daily routine, reach out to one person, and let yourself rest as well as search.
Notice your shoulders and jaw right now. Many of us hold work stress there without knowing it. Let them drop, and take one slow breath before your next task.
What is one boundary at work that would make your life easier? It might be not answering messages late at night. Think about how you could say it kindly this week.
Your colleagues are probably also tired and worried about their own things. A small word of thanks or a greeting can make the whole office feel lighter, including for you.
Burning out on a career you chose is not shameful. People change, and so do jobs. It is fine to ask what you want next, even if you are not ready to act on it yet.
Talk to someone you trust about how work is affecting you. You do not need a solution first. Saying it out loud often makes the problem smaller.
Small wins count. Finishing a report, replying to a hard email, showing up when you wanted to hide. Give yourself credit for one of them today.
Not every day will be productive, and that is normal. Aim for a good enough day. Do the essential things and let the rest be imperfect.
If you are worried about an upcoming appraisal, list three real things you achieved this year. Facts calm anxiety better than guesses do.
Pay or promotion delays can make you feel unseen. It is reasonable to ask for a meeting and calmly say what you have done and what you hope for next.
Work will always ask for more than one person can give. Choosing what to protect, like sleep, meals, and time with people you love, is not selfish. It keeps you able to keep going.
burnout: Being exhausted does not mean you are weak. It means you have carried a lot.
Rest is not a reward you must earn. You need it already.
Say no to one small thing today. Notice how it feels.
Ten minutes of quiet is a real break. Take them.
You are allowed to slow down.
Eat something real today. Skipped meals make everything harder.
Tired in a way sleep does not fix? That is worth listening to.
Switch off notifications for one hour today.
Your energy is limited. Spend it on what matters most.
Caring a lot and being drained can happen together.
Stretch your back and neck for one minute. Your body has been waiting.
Doing less today is not failing. It is protecting tomorrow.
Go to bed ten minutes earlier tonight.
Step outside for fresh air, even for two minutes.
Being needed everywhere is tiring. Remember that you are a person too.

Burnout often grows quietly. Small signs like dread, numbness, or constant irritation are your mind asking for care. Today, notice which sign is loudest for you, and treat it kindly. Listening early can save you a much harder season later.
Try a gentle reset today. Choose one task to drop, one to delay, and one to ask someone else to help with. You do not need to carry everything alone.
When everything feels pointless, it can be the exhaustion talking rather than the truth. Rest first, then look again at what matters to you.
It is easy to feel guilty for resting when others seem to cope. But coping on the outside can hide tiredness on the inside. You do not have to compare.

Think about what used to bring you joy before you got this tired. You do not have to do it today, just remember it. Joy is not gone, only waiting for energy to return. Start with five minutes this week and see how it feels.

If you are always on call for family, work, or friends, plan a small protected pocket of time this week. Tell people ahead that you will be unavailable and keep to it. People often respect a clear boundary more than you expect.

Long days, traffic, and uncertain money can wear anyone down. Be gentle with yourself about what you cannot finish. Finishing less does not make you less capable. On the hard days, doing the basics well is already plenty.
Ask yourself honestly: what is draining me most right now? You may not be able to remove it, but naming it is the first step to making it lighter.
Recovery is not a straight line. Some days you will feel better and then tired again. That is normal. Keep taking small steps, however slow they feel.
You do not need a holiday to begin recovering. Tiny things add up: a full glass of water, a walk, a laugh with a friend, a phone put down before bed.
Perfectionism can feed burnout. Today, let one thing be good enough instead of perfect, and see what happens to your stress level.
A message you can send to someone you trust: I have been very tired lately and I want to talk. You do not need to explain everything. Starting is enough.

Many caring people burn out because they put others first for too long. Helping others is good, but you cannot pour from an empty cup. Fill yours a little today. Looking after yourself is part of looking after them.
Try a slow breath: in for four counts, hold for two, out for six. Repeat five times. It tells your body it is safe to ease off the pressure.

Burnout can make you feel cynical or numb, as if nothing matters. That is a sign of overload, not a flaw in your character. Go gently and give yourself time. With rest, support, and time, the feeling of care usually finds its way back.
Look at your week and find one hour that is not for anyone else. Write it in. Protect it as you would an important meeting.
When you wake up already tired, start small. Sit up, drink water, wash your face. The goal is not a perfect day, only a gentle beginning.
It can help to separate who you are from what you produce. You are still valuable on days when you do very little.
Hustle culture says rest is laziness. It is not. Rest is how a body and mind repair themselves. You are allowed to repair.
Check in with yourself at midday. How is my body? How is my mood? What does it need now? Even a short answer can change the rest of your day.

If you can, spend a few minutes today with someone who makes you feel at ease, without talking about work or problems. Light company can be real medicine for the spirit. Let yourself be a person first and a helper second, just for a while.

Sleep is often the first thing we sacrifice and the first thing we need. Tonight, try to keep the phone away from your bed and give yourself time to wind down. Small changes in the evening can make a big difference by morning.

There may be things you cannot change right now, like your hours or your responsibilities. But you can change how you treat yourself within them. Be your own kind voice today. That kindness is one thing nobody can take from you.
You might feel guilty about slowing down. Guilt is a feeling, not a fact. You are not letting anyone down by looking after your health.
Take a short walk without your phone. Look at the trees, the sky, the street. Let your mind wander a little. It is a rest that costs nothing.

If tiredness has lasted a long time or is affecting your daily life, consider talking to a trusted person or a professional. You deserve support, not just endurance. There is no prize for suffering in silence.
List three things you are expected to do this week that no one would truly miss if they slipped. Give yourself permission to let them go.
Remember a time you felt rested and well. What was different then? Maybe you can bring back one small piece of it this week.
Being strong does not mean never needing a break. Even the strongest people stop to rest and refill.
Plan something small to look forward to this weekend: a favourite food, a visit, a nap. Having something ahead can make a heavy week lighter.

Today, try a single-task hour. Do only one thing, with phone away and no switching between tasks. It often feels calmer and gets more done than constant juggling. Notice how your body feels when you are not pulled in ten directions.

When others pile work on you because you always say yes, it is not only their fault. It is also a pattern you can change slowly, with small and polite boundaries. Practise one polite no this week and watch what happens.
Your body keeps count of every long week. Thank it today with something simple, like warm water, a good meal, or a slow stretch.
It is not too late to rest. Not this week, not this year. Look for one small way to ease your load today.
You have been carrying a lot for a long time. Sit for a moment and say to yourself: it makes sense that I am tired. Then let that be enough for now.
school: One page of revision is better than none. Start small.
Your result does not decide your worth.
Drink water and eat breakfast before you study. Your brain needs fuel.
It is okay to not understand a topic yet. Yet is the important word.
Study for twenty-five minutes, then rest for five. Try it today.
Comparing your marks with a friend's helps no one.
Sleep is part of studying. Do not skip it.
Write down just three things to learn today.
A bad test is one test. It is not your whole story.
Ask your teacher one question today, even a small one.
Take a break from your phone while you read.
Feeling nervous before exams is normal. It means you care.
Start with the topic you like least, for just ten minutes.
Breathe in slowly, out slowly. Then open your book.
You have passed hard days before. This one too will pass.

When revision feels huge, break it into small boxes. Write each topic on a line and tick it when done. Seeing the ticks reminds you that you are moving, even if slowly. Then take a short walk, and begin the next box when you are ready.

JAMB, WAEC, or university exams can feel like the whole future hangs on one paper. Try to remember that you have more than one path, even if it does not feel that way tonight. One exam is a step on a road, not the end of it.

If your family expects top marks, their pressure often comes from love and fear, even if it hurts. You can say: I am trying my best. Please be patient with me. Parents often soften when they hear honestly how you are feeling.

Reading the same page again and again may not help. Try closing the book and explaining it aloud in your own words. It shows you what you really know. Try it on one topic today and see how much you remember.

Cannot study because of noise, power cuts, or a crowded house? Try a quiet corner at a library, a church, or a friend's place, or study early in the morning before the day begins. A calm place, even a small one, can change how much you take in.
Mistakes in practice questions are useful. They show you where to spend your time. Do not hide from them, they are pointing the way.
If you failed an exam, you may feel shame. But failing a paper is an event, not an identity. Many successful people retook exams and found their way.
Group study can help, if the group stays on task. Choose one or two friends who encourage you and agree on a topic before you meet.
Before bed, spend two minutes writing down what you managed today, even if it was little. Ending the day with progress helps you rest better.
Do not wait until you feel motivated. Motivation often arrives after you begin. Open the book, read one paragraph, and see how you feel.
Pressure to choose a course or a career can feel unfair when you are still young. It is fine to say you are still thinking. You can learn as you go.
If you are overwhelmed, speak to someone: a teacher, a counsellor, a relative or a friend. You do not have to carry exam stress alone.
Studying all night usually costs more than it gives. Your memory works better after rest. Try to protect your sleep, especially before an exam.
The night before an exam, review lightly, pack your things, and go to bed. Last-minute cramming often raises fear more than it raises marks.
In the exam hall, if your mind goes blank, put down your pen, breathe slowly three times, and read the question again. Start with an answer you do know.
Your classmates may look calm, but many are as nervous as you are. Most people hide their fear. You are not alone in feeling it.
Set a small reward after studying, like your favourite snack, a short walk, or a chat with a friend. Rewards make hard work feel kinder.

Fear of disappointing your parents is heavy. Try to remember that they want you to be well, not only to pass. Talk to them about how you are feeling if you can. Honest conversation, even a short one, often lowers the pressure.

If a subject feels impossible, find another way to learn it. Use a video, a different textbook, or a patient friend. Sometimes it is the explanation that is the problem, not you. Try another way before you decide that you cannot do it.
Use past questions to practise. Time yourself, mark honestly, and note the topics that appear often. Practice turns fear into familiarity.

Waiting for results is hard. Try to fill the time with things that steady you: a walk, a chore, a good meal, time with people you like. Worrying will not change the grade. Be kind to yourself in the waiting.
Not everyone learns the same way or at the same speed. If you learn slowly, it does not mean you are less intelligent. It means you are building it carefully.
Make a simple timetable for this week. Include breaks, meals, and sleep. A plan on paper reduces the feeling that everything is waiting for you at once.

When you are far from home or living in a new town for school, loneliness and stress can add up. Reach out to one new person this week. A short greeting can start something. You do not have to be alone just because you are away from home.
Tell yourself today: I do not need to know everything. I need to learn what I can, one step at a time.
You are more than your CGPA, your JAMB score, or your WAEC result. Those are measures of one day or one season, not of your whole life.

Anxiety before a test can feel like a racing heart or a tight stomach. Place a hand on your chest, slow your breath, and remind yourself that the feeling will fade. It passes, and it does not mean you are unprepared.

Is a teacher or lecturer making things harder? Try to ask for a short meeting and explain what you are struggling with. Many are more willing to help than they appear. Most teachers remember the student who asked early.

Fees, books, and transport can make school stressful in ways that have nothing to do with studying. Be kind to yourself about this. You are doing a lot, not just studying. Be patient with yourself. You are carrying more than a syllabus.
Switch subjects every hour or so. Changing topics keeps your mind fresh and helps you remember more than one long block of the same material.
Doubt appears before many exams. Write down three reasons you can pass, such as the work you have already done, and read them again when doubt returns.
Missing a class or falling behind is not the end. Make a short list of what you missed, pick the most important one, and begin there today.
Try studying with a plain notebook and a pen instead of your phone. Fewer distractions often means fewer hours needed. Give it a week and see how your focus changes.
When someone says you will fail, remember that one person's opinion is not a prophecy. Prove them wrong quietly by doing the next small thing.

After your exam, do not go over every answer with friends. It rarely helps and often adds worry. Rest your mind and focus on the next paper. What is done is done. Your energy is better spent on the next paper.
anxiety: A worry is a thought, not a fact. Let it pass like a cloud.
Breathe in for four, out for six. Do it three times now.
Name five things you can see right now. Slowly.
Your body is trying to protect you. You can tell it that you are safe.
Feel your feet on the floor. Press down gently.
You do not have to solve tomorrow today.
Anxious feelings rise, peak, and fall. This one will too.
Drink some water and unclench your jaw.
What you fear is not always what will happen.
Slow down your shoulders. They have been up near your ears.
Being anxious does not make you weak or broken.
Hold something cold or warm in your hands and notice how it feels.
Ask: what is one thing I can do right now? Just one.
Be kind to yourself on a nervous day.
Say it slowly: I am here, and I am okay in this moment.

Try the five-four-three-two-one exercise. Name five things you see, four you can touch, three you hear, two you smell, and one you taste. It gently brings your mind back to the present. It takes about a minute and you can do it anywhere, even on a bus.

Anxiety often says: what if the worst happens? Try asking the other side too. What if it goes fine? What if I cope better than I expect? Both are possible, and the second is just as likely. Your mind may be unkind in predicting, but you are better at coping than it says.

If worries come at night, keep a notebook by your bed. Write each one down and tell yourself you will look at it in the morning. Your mind can stop guarding it. Many people find the page holds the worry so that the head does not have to.
Many Nigerians carry worries about money, family, and the future all at once. It is understandable to feel anxious. You do not have to be calm all the time, just a little kinder to yourself.

Try box breathing: in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four. Do it four times. Slow breathing tells your body that there is no emergency right now. It is simple, it is free, and you can do it anywhere.

Before a stressful event, spend a minute picturing yourself getting through it, not perfectly, but well enough. Imagine the end of the day, when it is done and you are resting. Seeing yourself cope often makes the real moment feel a little more familiar.

When your heart races, remind yourself that it is a feeling, not a danger. It is uncomfortable, but it will pass. Breathe slowly and let it settle in its own time. You have felt it before and you are still here.

Worry feels like doing something, but often it only drains you. Try asking: is this a problem I can act on today? If yes, take one step. If no, gently let it be for now. Putting the unsolvable down for a while is not giving up, it is resting.
Limit how much bad news you read today. You can stay informed without checking every hour. Your mind deserves some quiet between headlines and messages.

A tip for talking about anxiety: you can say, my mind has been very worried lately, and I would like you to just listen. People often want to help but need to know how. You are allowed to ask for what you need.
Moving your body can use up some of the nervous energy. A short walk, stretching, or even shaking out your hands can help.

Anxiety often grows when we avoid what scares us. Today, take one tiny step toward something you have been putting off, such as a phone call, a reply, or just opening the document. Small brave steps add up, and each one teaches your mind that you can cope.

Notice what your thoughts are saying and try adding the words I am having the thought that. I am having the thought that I will fail. It creates a little space between you and the worry. It is a small trick, but it can lessen the power of a frightening thought.
Too much tea, coffee, or energy drinks can make nervous feelings stronger for some people. Notice how you feel and consider what suits you best.
If you feel anxious for no clear reason, that happens to many people. You do not need a reason to deserve comfort. Take a few slow breaths and be gentle with yourself.
Make a short list of things that have gone well recently, even tiny ones. Anxiety tends to remember only the problems. Your list helps the whole picture.
If you are anxious in a crowded bus or market, try pressing your feet to the ground, looking at one fixed point, and breathing out slowly for longer than you breathe in.
Give your worry a time limit. Set aside ten minutes this evening to think about it fully. When it comes up earlier, tell it: not now, I will see you at six.

Anxiety can make small things feel huge. If something feels like too much, ask: how important will this be in a week? In a month? It can shrink a problem back to its real size. Perspective is not about ignoring your feelings, only keeping them the right size.
Place one hand on your chest and one on your belly. Breathe so that the lower hand moves more. It is a quiet way to calm your body.

Try not to fight the anxious feeling. Let it be there, like weather, while you continue with something small. Fighting often makes it stronger, and allowing it can make it fade. Thoughts and feelings rise and fall on their own when we give them room.

Sometimes anxiety shows up as stomach trouble, headaches, or a tight chest. These feelings are real, and being gentle with yourself often helps. If they worry you, speak to someone you trust or a health worker.
Tell one trusted person how you are feeling today. A worry shared is often lighter than a worry hidden.
Today, treat yourself as you would treat a nervous friend. What would you say to them? Say it to yourself.
Reassurance seeking, asking again and again if everything is okay, brings only short relief. Try sitting with the doubt for a few minutes and see that you can bear it.

Make your evening simple: dim the lights, put the phone down, and do one calming thing like a warm drink or a prayer or some soft music. Your mind learns that the day is ending. Doing this each night, even for a week, can make bedtime feel safer.
If you notice yourself imagining worst cases, pause and write down what you actually know right now. Facts are usually calmer than guesses.
You have been anxious before and you came through. That is real evidence that you can handle hard feelings, even when it does not feel like it.
Look around and find something blue. Then something round. Then something soft. Gentle games like this can steady your mind in a minute.
Take a pause before replying to a message that makes you nervous. Breathe, drink water, and then write. You are allowed to take your time.
Sometimes anxiety means we care about something important. Try asking what you care about, and what small, kind step might help you protect it.
Muscle tension builds quietly. Tighten your fists for five seconds, then release. Do the same with your shoulders and your feet. Feel the difference.
Not every anxious thought needs an answer. You can let some of them go by without chasing them.
When your worry is about something far away, bring yourself back to this hour. What do you need right now? A glass of water? A short rest? Start there.
There is help for anxiety, and asking for it is a strong thing to do. Talking with someone you trust, or a trained professional, can make it feel much lighter.
depression: Low moods pass, even when they feel endless. Be gentle with today.
Just getting up and washing your face counts as something.
Feeling better today is not required. Small is enough.
Open a window and let some light in.
Drink a glass of water. That is today's first win.
Heavy feelings are not a sign that you are failing.
One tiny step is still a step.
You matter, even on the days it is hard to believe.
Eat something, even if it is small.
Sit in the sun for a few minutes if you can.
Rest is not weakness. Your mind is carrying a lot.
Send one short message to someone who is kind to you.
Being tired of everything is a sign of pain, not of fault. You are not a burden.
Make your bed or tidy one small corner. Then stop.
Slow days are allowed.

Depression can make everything feel grey and far away. That does not mean it is the truth about your life. Try one small, kind thing today, like a warm drink or a short walk to the gate. You do not have to enjoy it, only begin.

Some days feel like climbing a hill. Shrink the hill. Make a list of only three things: eat, wash, and one thing you enjoy a little. That is a full day when you are low. Even on low days, you can count that as enough.

It is easy to be hard on yourself for not doing more. But you are doing something difficult every day just by continuing. Say that to yourself: I am doing something hard, and I am still here. That is not nothing. That is courage in a quiet form.
If you ever feel that you might hurt yourself, please tell someone you trust right away, or contact your local emergency services. You deserve help and you do not have to face it alone.
Low moods can make you pull away from people. If you can, send one word to a friend or relative today, like hello. You do not have to explain anything.

When your mind says that nothing will change, remember that feelings are not fixed. Moods move, sometimes slowly, sometimes in a sudden gentle way. Today does not have to be a forecast for tomorrow. Be patient. Change often comes quietly.

Not being able to do the things you used to enjoy does not mean you have lost them forever. Interest often returns slowly. For now, try something small for just five minutes. Five minutes is still five minutes toward feeling like yourself again.
Try a very short walk, to the gate or the end of the street. You do not need to go far. Fresh air and movement can ease the heaviness, even a little.

If you are feeling like you might be in danger from your own thoughts, please speak to someone you trust, or reach your local emergency services straight away. Your life is worth protecting. Reaching out in that moment is the bravest thing you can do.
It is not your fault that you feel this way, and you did not choose it. You can, however, choose small kindnesses to yourself while it lasts.
A way to talk to someone: I have not been feeling like myself, and I would like you to just sit with me. You do not need to have the right words. Being heard can help a lot.
Sleep and mood affect each other. If you can, try to go to bed and wake at similar times. Even small regular habits can give the days a gentle shape.

Your thoughts may be very harsh on you right now. They are thoughts, not facts. Would you say them to a friend who was hurting? Try speaking to yourself the way you would to them. Try speaking to yourself with the gentleness you would give a friend.
Faith, community, music, or prayer can bring comfort for some people. If any of these help you, lean on them today. There is no shame in holding onto what steadies you.

It is worth speaking to a doctor, counsellor, or trusted health worker. Asking for help is not weakness. It is looking after yourself. And if you ever feel that you might hurt yourself, please tell someone you trust or contact local emergency services right away.

Think of one person who would be glad to hear from you. Perhaps it is a sibling, an old friend, or a cousin. Reaching out can lift the loneliness a little for both of you. A short message is enough to start.

On days when everything feels pointless, try noticing one small thing that is not painful: the taste of tea, the sound of rain, a child laughing outside. Let it stay for a moment. Notice it, and let that be enough for now.
When thoughts of hurting yourself ever come, please do not keep them alone. Tell a person you trust or contact local emergency services right now. Help is real, and you are worth it.
Comparing yourself to others on social media can sink you further. Today, try taking a break from it and see how your mind feels.
Bad days do not erase the good ones. They are real, and they will return. Keep going gently.

When your energy is very low, choose the smallest possible version of a task. Not a full bath, but washing your face. Not a full meal, but a piece of fruit. Small versions count. Do what you can, and let the rest wait.
Many people have felt what you are feeling, though few say it aloud. You are not alone, even if the feeling says you are.
Feeling numb rather than sad can be confusing. Numbness is also part of low mood. Let yourself be as you are, and do one soft thing today.
Heavy mornings are common with low mood. If today is one of them, begin with only one action: sit up. Then wait a moment. Then another small thing. No rush.
Money worries, family pressure, and loss can pile up and press hard. Be patient with yourself while you carry all of that. You are not behind in some race.
When someone tells you to just be strong or cheer up, know that they may not understand. What you are feeling is real, and you do not need to hide it to be acceptable.
Try listening to a song you used to like. Music can sometimes reach us when words cannot. Let it play without asking anything of yourself.
Write down one sentence about how you are today, with no editing. Putting feelings on paper can make them a bit less tangled.

Staying in bed most of the day is common with low mood. Try to change one thing, like moving to a chair, sitting by a window, or taking a few steps. Small changes can nudge the day. Even small movements remind your body that it can change.
Allow yourself to cry if you need to. Tears can release some of the weight. It is not weakness, it is a human response to pain.

Do not wait to feel ready before asking for help. People who care often want to help but do not know you are hurting. Letting them know is a gift to both of you. Reaching out is something you are allowed to do before you feel ready.
If you ever feel that you might act on thoughts of ending your life, please tell someone near you or call your local emergency services immediately. You do not have to carry this alone.
Think of one thing that has gotten you through before, a person, a habit, a prayer. Reach for it a little today.
Healing from low mood is often slow and uneven. A better hour is still a better hour. Notice it when it comes.
Every hard day you have had so far, you have survived. That is a quiet kind of strength, even when you do not feel strong.
stress: You do not have to solve the whole week today.
Breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in. Do it three times.
Rest is part of the work, not a reward for finishing it.
Pick one task. Only one. Start there.
Your shoulders may be higher than they need to be. Let them drop.
Not every problem needs an answer before lunch.
Drink some water before you face the day.
Feeling overwhelmed means you are carrying a lot, not that you are failing.
Ten quiet minutes can change how a hard day feels.
Say no to one small thing today.
Tomorrow's worries can wait until tomorrow.
A short walk counts as a break.
Slow is still moving.
Eat something real today, even if you are busy.
Today only needs your best, not everything.
When light goes off, traffic eats your morning and money feels tight, stress is a normal response. Name what weighs on you, then choose one thing you can actually influence.
Write down everything on your mind, even the small things. A list on paper is lighter than a list in your head.
If your phone makes you tense, keep it away for the first fifteen minutes after you wake. Let your mind arrive before the news does.
Stress often tells us what we care about. Ask which worry matters most today, and let the others be quieter for now.
Between tasks, stop for one minute. Close your eyes, feel your feet on the floor, and notice three sounds around you.
You may be trying to be strong for everyone at home. Who can be strong for you this week? Consider telling one person how heavy things are.
Money pressure is one of the heaviest kinds of stress. You do not need a full plan today. Just write down one small next step, such as a call to make or a number to check.
If your mind races at night, keep a notebook by your bed. Write the worry down and tell yourself you will look at it in the morning.
Your body shows stress through headaches, tight jaws and tired eyes. Notice one sign today and answer it kindly with water, a stretch or a pause.
Being busy is not the same as being productive. Choose the three things that matter most today and let the rest wait without guilt.
It is okay to take a moment in the bathroom, the car or a quiet corner just to breathe. Small private pauses are allowed.
What would you say to a friend who had your exact day? Try saying a little of that to yourself.
When people ask how you are, you can say something more honest than fine. Try: I have had a lot on my mind. See how it feels.
Stress grows when we carry it alone. Today, share one worry with someone you trust, or bring it to a Therapia chat room.
Notice what you do when stressed: scroll, snack, snap at people. No judgement. Awareness is the first step to choosing something gentler.
Some pressure comes from work, from family, from the community. Which expectations are really yours, and which did you inherit?
Breathe in for four counts, hold for two, breathe out for six. Repeat five times. It tells your body it is safe enough to slow down.
A bad morning does not have to become a bad day. Take a small reset at midday: wash your face, stretch, drink water, then begin again.
Make the first hour of your day small and calm if you can. Even ten quiet minutes before the rush sets a different tone.
Deadlines, bills and family needs can pile up. Break one big thing into pieces so small they feel almost silly. Do the first piece.

Try a five-minute reset today. Sit down, put both feet flat on the floor, and place one hand on your chest. Breathe slowly and name what you feel without fixing it: tight, worried, tired. Naming a feeling often loosens its grip. When the five minutes end, choose one small thing to do next.

Many of us were taught that being tired means being weak, and that a good person keeps going no matter what. But a body and mind under constant pressure need recovery, just like a phone needs charging. Where in your day can you plug in, even for a few minutes? Protect that small space.

Sort your worries into two groups today. In the first, put things you can act on, like a bill to discuss or a message to send. In the second, put things you cannot control, like other people's opinions or the traffic. Give your energy to the first group, and practise letting the second one sit.

When everything feels urgent, nothing gets done well. Look at your list and ask three questions: What must happen today? What can happen tomorrow? What can I drop completely? You may be surprised how much of the pressure comes from things that do not truly need you today.

Far from home and working hard in a new city, stress can come with loneliness attached. It is okay to feel both. Call someone who knows you well, even for five minutes, and let yourself be a person rather than a worker. You do not have to keep performing.

Stress can make us believe we must fix everything immediately. Set a timer for ten minutes and give one problem your full attention. When the timer ends, stop, even if it is unfinished. Often the problem feels smaller once you have touched it.

Think of a time you went through a stressful season and came out the other side. What helped you then? A person, a routine, a prayer, a good meal, a walk? Write it down. You have survived hard days before, and some of those tools may still be within reach today.

Evening can be a good time to close the day on purpose. Put your phone down, write one line about what went well and one thing for tomorrow, then stop thinking about work. Your mind needs a clear signal that the day is over, or it will keep working through the night.

Sometimes stress is a sign that something needs to change, not just something to endure. Ask yourself gently: is it the workload, a relationship, money, or too little rest? You do not have to change everything. Choosing one thing to adjust, or one person to ask for help, is enough for now.

Comparing your life with posts you see online can add a quiet layer of stress. People show their best moments, not their bills or sleepless nights. Today, spend a little less time looking at other lives, and a little more time noticing one thing in your own that is steady and good.

If you feel overwhelmed right now, try the five, four, three, two, one exercise. Name five things you see, four you can touch, three you hear, two you smell and one you taste. It slowly brings your attention back from the worry to the present moment, where you are safe enough.

Asking for help is a skill, not a weakness. This week, try one specific request, such as: Can you watch the children for an hour? Or: Can you listen to me for ten minutes? Specific requests are easier to say yes to, and you may find more support around you than you expected.

You have probably been running on adrenaline for a while. A pause may feel strange at first, even guilty. That is normal. Give yourself permission to do one thing today only because it brings you calm: a cup of tea, music, a quiet sit outside. Calm is not laziness. It is how you refill.

Faith can be a real source of steadiness during stress. If prayer or reflection helps you, take a few minutes today, even in a quiet corner. If words feel hard, simply sitting still counts. Pair it with practical care too, like food, sleep and talking to someone you trust.

Stress does not mean you are doing life wrongly. It means you are dealing with real demands. Be fair to yourself: list what you have handled in the past month, even the small things. Seeing it on paper may remind you how much you have carried, and how capable you have been.
loneliness: Feeling lonely does not mean something is wrong with you.
Send one message today to someone you have not spoken to in a while.
Loneliness is a signal, like hunger. It points to a need for connection.
A simple greeting to a neighbour counts as connection.
You can be surrounded by people and still feel alone. Many people do.
Call someone instead of texting today.
Being alone and being lonely are not the same thing.
Small moments of contact add up.
Step outside for a few minutes. Let other people's life be around you.
Someone else is probably hoping you will reach out first.
Your need for company is human, not a burden.
Share one true thing about your day with someone.
Evenings can feel the longest. Plan one small thing for tonight.
A voice note can warm a quiet room.
You are allowed to take up space in someone's life.
Living far from family can make the days feel quiet. Try a short call home this week, even if you only talk about food and small news.
Join a Therapia group meeting when you feel ready. You can listen without speaking, and you will hear others describing feelings much like yours.
Pick one person from your past, a school friend or an old colleague, and send a simple message: I thought of you today. How are you?
Loneliness can make us think everyone else is busy and happy. Most people carry private gaps too. Your reaching out may be a relief to them.
Look for a regular place to belong: a church or mosque group, a sports club, a community class. Familiar faces build slowly, and showing up again and again is the key.
If chatting feels like too much, try the Therapia chat rooms. You can share a little at your own pace and be heard by people who understand.
Notice who you meet in a normal day: the seller at the market, the driver, the colleague. A warm word with each one is a small thread of connection.
Weekends and holidays can feel empty when others have plans. Make a small plan of your own, like a walk, a meal you enjoy or a call with someone far away.
Social media can make loneliness louder. If scrolling leaves you feeling left out, put the phone down and do one thing with your hands instead.
Ask someone a real question today, not just how are you. Something like: What has been the best part of your week? Good questions open doors.
